strengths: NC-OOD is a simple, potentially useful post-hoc detector. Equation 5 reuses classifier weights and a global feature mean, avoiding nearest-neighbor searches, covariance estimation, and storage of individual training features. Its low additional computational cost is a meaningful practical contribution.

The evaluation spans CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, ResNet and DenseNet architectures, and cross-entropy and supervised contrastive training. Selecting alpha using Gaussian noise rather than the benchmark OOD datasets is a positive experimental choice.

The reported ResNet results are competitive: Table 1 gives average AUROC of 95.36 versus KNN's 94.92 on CIFAR-10, and 94.15 versus DICE+ReAct's 93.40 on ImageNet. CIFAR-10 FPR95 also improves from 29.31 to 25.94. Under supervised contrastive training, NC-OOD achieves 98.10 AUROC and 9.84 FPR95, compared with KNN+'s 97.95 and 11.61.

The component ablation provides substantial evidence for combining alignment and magnitude. On ImageNet, Table 4 reports 94.15 AUROC for NCScore versus 88.69 for pScore and 87.08 for the L1 norm. The alternative similarity scores and supplementary CIFAR-10 ablations further help characterize the method.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not valid under its stated assumptions. Equation 3 concerns normalized vectors; obtaining the unnormalized convergence in Equation 1 requires additional control of feature norms and convergence rates. For example, with two classes having features/means ±t e1 and weights ±(t e1+e2), NC1 holds exactly and NC3 holds asymptotically, but the residual norm in Equation 1 tends to 1. A weaker directional statement remains useful and this issue does not invalidate the empirical detector, but it reduces the claimed theoretical contribution. Training-set collapse also does not establish separation of unseen ID and OOD samples.

The distinct contribution of the neural-collapse interpretation is insufficiently isolated. Algebraically, pScore is a centered, feature-normalized predicted-class logit, and combining similarity with feature magnitude already appears in the cited CSI work. Comparisons against normalized-logit and class-mean prototype scores would clarify what using classifier weights specifically contributes. Relevant post-hoc methods such as ViM (CVPR 2022) and ASH (ICLR 2023) are also absent, weakening the state-of-the-art positioning.

The evidence supports broad competitiveness more strongly than consistent superiority. In Table 3, NC-OOD trails KNN on DenseNet/CIFAR-10 AUROC, 96.89 versus 97.20, and DICE+ReAct on DenseNet/CIFAR-100, 86.18 versus 86.79. On CIFAR-100, its FPR95 is substantially worse than KNN's, 62.62 versus 47.36. ImageNet FPR95 is essentially tied with DICE+ReAct, 27.28 versus 27.25. No uncertainty estimates are provided for the relatively small average AUROC gains.

There are reporting inconsistencies that affect interpretation. In Table 10, ReAct+DICE's six FPR95 entries average 45.00, whereas the reported average is 76.45; correcting this reverses its comparison with NC-OOD's 62.62. Section 4.4.1 also claims pScore consistently outperforms KNN across ImageNet OOD sets, but Texture AUROC is 91.96 for pScore versus 97.07 for KNN. These are correctable issues, but they matter more than typographical refinements because they overstate comparative performance.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence remain incomplete. Although Section 7 references supplementary code, the supplied PDF does not specify important details such as KNN's neighborhood/subsampling configuration, training of the supervised-contrastive classifier head, or the Gaussian validation protocol sufficiently precisely. No timing or memory measurements substantiate the claimed rapid inference. Overall, the useful lightweight detector and positive experimental results place the paper near acceptance, while the theoretical overstatement, incomplete isolation of novelty, and comparative-evidence concerns keep the recommendation borderline.
